The preceding exposition of the five matters contained two verses; the first verse has already been divided into ten sections.
The separate section concludes.
From here below is the second part, which analyzes [the subject] by means of twelve gates.
Within this, first, one verse is cited to list those eleven gates.
Next, the gates will be explained according to their sequence.
Regarding the different ways the number of gates in the verse is opened and closed,
Master Jing judges as follows:
There are ten sections.
First is the analytical investigation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
which provides two explanations.
First interpretation:
Because it is able to discern and grasp various categories such as the "appropriating aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*), it is called the "nature of discernment" (*pravicaya-svabhāva*).
According to this interpretation, the "nature of discernment" serves as the general heading.
Taking the *Sakya* [text], the following nine gates are correctly enumerated.
Second is the explanation;
the first gate is "Investigation."
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) constitutes the second gate.
Therefore, in the prose section, the question "Regarding all those phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*), they should be said...
and what follows explains this second gate.
If one follows this interpretation, there are eleven sections;
however, in the present case, there are ninety-one sections, all of which are fully contained within the subsequent interpretation.
Discernment is the first;
intrinsic nature is the second;
grasping is the third.
Sāṃkhya is the fourth;
Āstika is the fifth;
Lokāyata is the sixth.
Truth is the seventh;
investigation and analysis are the eighth;
and thorough knowledge is the ninth.
The tenth is the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*);
the eleventh is the sequential order.
Within the explanation according to the gates, there are briefly nine sections.
This is because the existence of the *satkāya* and one portion of the world are explained in conjunction.
First, regarding the initial gate, the inclusion of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths is clarified;
subsequently, they are analyzed according to their numerical categories.

Regarding the preceding statement that "the characteristics are subsumed under the four established truths," this contradicts the previous discussion which stated that the characteristics of the truths are subsumed under both the established (*prajñapti*) and non-established (*aprajñapti*) truths.
The characteristic has two meanings: broad and narrow.
When it is said that the three truths are distinguished and the truth of cessation is excluded, this very text states that the truth of the path is included within the distinction.
Within this discernment (*vikalpa*), there are the stages of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
These—the path of means (*upāyamārga*) and the path of provisions (*sambhāramārga*)—are collectively subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
This discernment itself constitutes the truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*).
Regarding the statement that "True Suchness (tathatā) is not subsumed under the four established truths":
this means that True Suchness, which is the equality of the four truths, is subsumed under the non-established truth (apratiṣṭhita-satya).
As Master Tai’s chapter states:
Just as previously there was the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), [the analysis] here concerns only the contaminated;
now, however, it is said that the analysis pertains to what is subsumed within the three truths (*satya*).
According to the treatises, it is said that there are five truths of the path (*mārgasatya*),
which include those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
As for True Suchness (*tathatā*) being subsumed under the four non-established truths (*avyavasthāpita-satya*):
Because this is the true suchness (*tathatā*) of reality, it is called "the fourfold.
Since it cannot be established as cause and effect,
it is said to be "non-established" (*avyavasthāpana*).
The following section on the enumeration of categories consists of five question-and-answer pairs.
The first question-and-answer pair concerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and names (*nāman*), etc.
[It asks: "Are all names characteristics? And are there characteristics that are not names?"
Because a broad question was asked regarding something narrow, the answer follows the latter part of the verse.
This passage means that all five dharmas are termed "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
As for the phrase "the others as appropriate," etc.:
By means of the three— relative, discriminative,

and so forth— and furthermore, by correlating "name" with the latter three up to "suchness" (tathatā) with "correct wisdom" (samyagjñāna), the pattern of correspondence and exclusion is likewise applied.
This concludes the second question-and-answer section concerning characteristics and the characteristics of characteristics.
The five entities possess substantiality and are collectively termed "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Among these five, the first characteristic enumerates all five names; therefore, it is called the "characteristic of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Answer: All characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are indeed characteristics.
However, there may be characteristics that are not the primary characteristic of characteristics; these refer to the other four characteristics, such as "name" (nāman) and so forth.
This is also an answer by way of the subsequent clause (anuloma-paścāt-pada).
The third question and answer:
A fourfold analysis regarding characteristics and names.
If one analyzes the characteristic of the initial characteristic, [it is as follows].
Are all things such that, when a second name and characteristic are designated, they mutually combine and depend upon one another to give rise to a discriminating mind?
Furthermore, when a second name and characteristic is conceptually distinguished, [is it likewise so?]
Are all these initial characteristics mutually combined with the second characteristic, and do they arise through mutual conjunction and mutual dependence as conceptual constructions?
Answer: There are initial characteristics that are conceptual constructions.
It is not by means of a second name or characteristic that they mutually combine and depend upon one another to give rise to conceptual discrimination—
such as the discriminating minds of cattle, sheep, or infants—
which cannot comprehend the primary characteristics of those names.
Furthermore, from the first bhūmi upward,
all bodhisattvas have already uprooted the latent tendencies of the attachment to dharmas— the linguistic permeations of names that underlie the definitive meanings within all phenomena.
When bodhisattvas take the characteristics of various characteristics as their object, they do not grasp those characteristics by relying on their names and expressions.
Second, there is "conceptualization" (vikalpa), which refers to the characteristic of naming;
it does not mean that the initial characteristic and the characteristic of naming mutually combine or depend upon one another to give rise to conceptualization.
This refers to when a person from another country first arrives in a foreign land and,
being unable to discern the characteristics and phenomena of names and signs,
understands linguistic conventions in a manner contrary to the three aforementioned [correct] ways.
Generally, taking the name based on the characteristic and taking the characteristic based on the name constitutes the "both" category (*ubhaya-pada*).
When the fourfold non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) discards both name and characteristic,
this is the "neither" category (*anubhaya-pada*), excluding all such aforementioned characteristics.
The fourth question and answer concerns the four propositions regarding the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness). Jing says:
"If one contemplates *tathatā* yet does not even perceive the actual *tathatā*..."
At the time when one seeks to realize true suchness through both preparatory application and subsequently attained wisdom,
there arises an appearance resembling true suchness that manifests within the mind;
however, actual suchness is not seen.
"Descending from its own level" refers to the stage prior to full penetration and the stage of subsequent reflection upon the established nature of suchness (*tathatā*).
This includes those who contemplate suchness and proceed to reflect upon its characteristics.
Non-conceptual wisdom that directly realizes [suchness] is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
It is not a conceptualization that grasps the marks of suchness through discursive thought;
nevertheless, there arises an effort associated with mental attention (manasikāra).
It is said that mental attention (*manasikāra*) is what is called "reflection" (*cintā*).
Therefore, it is stated that one reflects upon its characteristics from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "the subsequent continuous reflection that penetrates the non-conceptually-constructed (*aprapañcita*) suchness," this refers to the following.
After its initial manifestation, it is said to be continuous.
True wisdom arises and reflexively contemplates the true suchness (tathatā) perceived within meditative observation;
because it is guided by realized knowledge, it remains vividly clear to itself.
"Neither [of the two]" refers to being free from the mental attention that contemplates various signs (*nimitta*).
Tai says: "This is contemplating true suchness (*tathatā*), not seeing true suchness."

This means that on the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, from the stage of "correct mental attention" (yoniśomanasikāra) subsumed under the second type of discrimination up to the stage of "patience" (kṣānti), one contemplates the principle of the signlessness and emptiness of objects;
at the stage of "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma), one contemplates the principle of the non-arising and emptiness of consciousness.
This refers to the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*).
To perceive only the characteristics of the reflected image of true suchness is to be subsumed under the first characteristic;
it does not mean perceiving the fourth reality, the true suchness of the fundamental nature.
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment up until the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
one has not yet reached the state of direct penetration into *tathatā* (suchness) belonging to the first bhūmi;
nor has one reached the direct penetration into *tathatā* by means of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) from the first bhūmi upward.
Subsequently, one contemplates suchness with the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Emerging from meditative absorption through that subsequently attained wisdom,
one again deliberately attends to and contemplates the image-like appearance of the established suchness.
This is also the mutual inclusion of the initial characteristics,
because one attends to and contemplates the fourth true suchness (tathatā) with mental attention;
thus, it is called "contemplating true suchness."
However, in this contemplation, one contemplates only the appearance of the initial signs;
one does not see the fourth reality, true suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the second phrase, there is contemplation of true suchness, yet it is not conceptualization of true suchness.
This means that from the first bhūmi upward, when the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) penetrates suchness, it does so by way of ultimate truth;
meanwhile, within the preparatory wisdom (prayoga-jñāna), one contemplates its initial characteristics.
That which is unattainable is precisely the entry into the contemplation of the wisdom of the ultimate essence (*samyag-jñāna*), wherein one perceives the true *tathatā*.
This is because the first characteristic is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—which is said to exist—while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is said to be non-existent.
As for the third phrase, it refers to that which follows after all wisdoms of the ultimate essence have thoroughly penetrated *tathatā*.

The continuity [of this process] is the subsequent attainment wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which repeatedly contemplates the principle of suchness as the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
Regarding this, there are two interpretations in the West (India).
The first interpretation states:
The subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) that continues [from meditative equipoise] contemplates suchness;
because it is an observation of suchness in which no images appear,
it is called "contemplating suchness."
The second explanation states:
Although the wisdom attained after [meditative equipoise] possesses the aspect of images, its contemplation of suchness is subsumed under the first aspect;
nevertheless, it resembles the suchness of the original nature-aspect.
Therefore, it is called the contemplation of non-established suchness (*apratiṣṭhita-tathatā*).
The first phrase above separately involves further mental reflection on established suchness (*pratiṣṭhita-tathatā*),
which does not correspond to the suchness that is the true nature of reality.
Therefore, it is called "not contemplating suchness.
As for the fourth phrase,
it refers to being apart from the mental attention induced by correct reasoning, which is distinct from various signs.
He does not contemplate the characteristics of *tathatā*. Bei states:
"Contemplation has conceptual mental attention as its essence."
Because it involves conceptual discrimination, it is certainly not the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) associated with mental attention has wisdom as its essence.
The wisdom that realizes suchness (*tathatā*), along with that which takes as its object phenomena appearing as characteristics, is collectively termed "contemplation."
Since contemplation and reflection differ,
four propositions are established.
The first proposition consists of the preparatory wisdom prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that takes conventional designations as its object.
The second phrase refers to the wisdom of the true nature (samyaktva-jñāna).
The third phrase refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) which takes the non-conceptually-constructed (apratiṣṭhita) as its object.
Question: For what reason is the subsequently attained wisdom that takes suchness (tathatā) as its object in the first phrase called "conceptually-constructed" (pratiṣṭhita)?
Regarding the statement that "the suchness which is the object of focus in the third phrase is called non-established":

the commentary explains that the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) elucidated in the third phrase is so designated because it arises sequentially from the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna).
It is the non-established suchness (*apratiṣṭhita-tathatā*).
Regarding the first phrase, the suchness that is the object of focus is called "established" because it does not resemble its own essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Question: What is the ontological nature (*dharmatā*) of the subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata?
The commentary states:
There are two views in the Western lands (India).
One view holds that the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata never takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
Why is this? Because if one takes reality as the object of focus, one immediately realizes suchness;
therefore, it is called the wisdom of the fundamental essence (mūla-jñāna).

One explanation holds that subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) also takes both the ultimate and conventional as its objects. However, this subsequently attained wisdom is of two kinds:
first, within a single moment of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the objects are distinguished as the two types of wisdom.
If it is as such, [the first case] exclusively takes principle (li) as its object.
Second, there is subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) which takes conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the characteristics of suchness (tathatā-lakṣaṇa) as its objects.
The fourth phrase excludes the mental application that takes principle as its object.
The other modes of attention take this fourfold tetralemma of suchness as their primary object; therefore,
they are called the "True Fourfold Tetralemma."
Master Ji says:
The first phrase [indicates that] the preparatory wisdom prior to the stages (bhūmi) possesses conceptual discrimination.
Because the aspect of the suchness that is the object of focus does not resemble the essential nature of suchness,
it is not called "contemplating suchness.
This is the second phrase.
Because the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is non-conceptual and realizes suchness (*tathatā*), it is [the subject of] the question and answer.
If that is so, why is it called "contemplation" (*manasikāra*)?
The commentary states:
This is not the same as the preceding contemplation;
for instance, the untainted *manas* is termed "mind" (*manas*).
It is not called "volition" because it is not defiled volition;
yet, because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is also named "volition.

The third category refers to that which is induced by the subsequent cognition following the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the first stage and above, taking true suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
The object of subsequently attained wisdom appears as the semblance of suchness;
because it closely resembles suchness, it is termed "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
Because it involves conceptual discrimination, it is termed "reflection" (cintā).
In the *Tattvārtha-śāstra*, that which takes the object of focus (ālambana) as its name is called "non-established" (*apratiṣṭhita*).
The fourth phrase refers to all mental attentions (*manasikāra*) other than those directed toward the principle (*nyāya*).
The detailed analysis of the remaining meanings is the same as that of Master Bei.
Jingyun: Contemplation has two meanings.
First, because it emphasizes observation.
Second, because it is not true contemplation.
"Contemplation" (guan) carries the meaning of penetrating realization and illuminating observation.
However, this refers even to the third phrase, which speaks of contemplating and reflecting upon True Suchness (tathatā).
This refers to the right knowledge of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is called "reflection" (*manasikāra*) because it involves repeated contemplation,
and it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because it involves clear observation.
According to the meaning, in ancient times the cultivation of the path was called "contemplation" (思惟).
Now, among various commentaries, the explanation by Sthiramati is superior.
However, if one follows the master Nanda:
Because the fundamental essence of true wisdom within the central reality does not cultivate the original substance as real,
it transforms into other images;
this is inconsistent with the present text.
Regarding the fourfold logical propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the "corresponding characteristics" (*junsō*), there is still a sequential order.
The fifth question and answer concerns the fourfold propositions based on the contemplation of the characteristics of corresponding characteristics. Jing says:
The preceding four phrases are reversed.
Regarding the phrase "there is the characteristic of contemplation, yet one does not observe its characteristic," which refers to the second phrase above:
this is the contemplation of the characteristic of true thusness (tathatā) that is free from characteristics.
It is not a matter of grasping at signs while contemplating the characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā).
Rather, it is as previously mentioned: contemplating without mental engagement (amanasikāra).
There is the contemplation of its characteristic, yet no mental engagement with that characteristic.
The preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) that previously sought true suchness (*tathatā*) was unable to realize it directly;
furthermore, the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) still takes suchness as its object and observes it by grasping its characteristics (*nimitta*).
Regarding the observation of its characteristics through contemplation, "its characteristics" refers to the fourth phrase mentioned above.
This means being free from the mental attention that contemplates signs as they are logically induced;
it is precisely not contemplating *tathatā* (suchness) nor observing *tathatā*.
There is a case where there is neither contemplation of signs nor observation of their signs, which refers to the aforementioned third phrase.
This refers to contemplating the non-established truth of *tathatā* within the mind of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) after first emerging from meditative absorption;
it does not involve conceptualizing or observing the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. Jing says:
The second phrase refers to contemplating its characteristics alone;
because it is ultimately unattainable according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
it is called "contemplating characteristics."
At that time, because one who is signless perceives only suchness and does not perceive signs,
it is called "not contemplating its signs.
The first phrase [of the preceding section] refers to contemplating and perceiving the aspect of suchness.
Among these, this is the first sign:
at that time, one contemplates True Suchness (tathatā),
but does not contemplate the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of True Suchness.
The first part of the fourth phrase— contemplating the initial characteristic and also observing the initial characteristic—
is easy to understand.
The first part of the third phrase— contemplating true suchness with wisdom and observing true suchness with attachment— is as follows.
Therefore, it is not conceptualization (*vitarka*). Furthermore, the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the five objects are also not the initial characteristic of observation (*vicāra*).
This is proven by this fourth phrase.

Therefore, it is known that even the conceptualizing mind of the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) described in the third phrase of the preceding section contemplates the actual *tathatā* with attachment.
This is because the *tathatā* as a reflected image corresponds to the *tathatā* of the essential nature and characteristics within the preceding contemplation.
Therefore, it is called "contemplating true suchness.
Because those prior to the stages have not yet attained penetration of true suchness, they do not [perceive] its marks;
although there are appearances resembling true suchness within the contemplation of non-arising, [they are not the actual suchness].
Because the present [state] does not accord with true suchness (tathatā), one does not contemplate true suchness. Bei said:
In this context, contemplation (cintā) is associated with both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Mental application (*manasikāra*), preparatory wisdom, subsequently attained wisdom, and all discerning prajñā are termed "insight" (*vipaśyanā*);
furthermore, they do not grasp at objects that take principles as their conditions.
Since there are these distinctions within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Although *tathatā* (suchness) is included among these four permutations, it is treated as the objective aspect (*nimitta*) and thus serves as the subject of the proposition.
The fourfold set of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) should be understood as the inverse of the preceding;
Master Ji’s intention is the same as that of [Daoshi] Bei.
Regarding the first statement, "there is the characteristic of conceptualization (*vitarka*) yet one does not contemplate its characteristic," this refers to the second phrase of the preceding [set].
This clarifies that the wisdom of the true essence contemplates the substance and characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness),
without observing any characteristics external to *tathatā*.
Regarding the second phrase, "there is observation of its characteristics but no contemplation of characteristics," this refers to the aforementioned first phrase.
This clarifies that while one contemplates various characteristics, one does not contemplate the essential nature or characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the third [stage], which involves both contemplating characteristics and observing their characteristics:
this clarifies both the contemplation of various characteristics and the observation of those characteristics.
The fourth [case], which is neither characterized by reflection (*vitarka*) nor by investigation (*vicāra*), refers to the aforementioned third phrase.
This clarifies that while taking an appearance resembling *tathatā* as an object, one does not reflect upon external characteristics nor investigate them.
The second is the section explaining the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within this, there are initially three questions and answers,
which constitute the formal thesis (*pratijñā*).
The latter section refutes external attachments.
Within the first part, the initial question and answer distinguish how all phenomena are subsumed within five categories. Jing says:
In truth, one should answer that it "encompasses all phenomena.
Yet, [the interlocutor] answers, "It is so."
The Sanskrit original therefore provides this answer.
The *Śāstra* states:
"All phenomena are subsumed within five categories."
Therefore, the five categories encompass all phenomena.
Since the thoroughly imagined nature is a non-existent entity— like the horns of a rabbit—
it is not encompassed by these five categories.
The second question and answer correctly distinguishes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Jing states: "Common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) can be described;
however, because the intrinsic nature transcends language, it cannot be described."
In this chapter, it further states that the way of verbal expression merely describes the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is beyond words and cannot be expressed. For example, although the term "blue" excludes yellow, red, and white, [it still does not express the ineffable nature].
However, the term "blue" applies generally to the entire blue dharma-realm, as the roots, stems, branches, and leaves of all blue bamboo are blue;
furthermore, by specifically mentioning "blue leaves," one distinguishes them from the roots, stems, and branches.
However, while the name "blue leaf" applies generally across its own dharma-realm,
each individual leaf has its own specific characteristics that do not resemble one another;
thus, although the name "one blue leaf" applies generally within its own dharma-realm, it does not resemble [the others].
Therefore, a single general name cannot distinguish the individual characteristics of each leaf within its own dharma-realm,
because the self-characteristics of each leaf in the dharma-realm are mutually dissimilar,
just as human faces are dissimilar from one another.
Within a single green leaf there are numerous atoms;
since none of these numerous atoms are themselves the green leaf,
the name "green leaf" likewise does not correspond to the actual phenomenon.
Furthermore, the individual characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of the numerous atoms are each dissimilar,
just like human faces; thus,
even the individual characteristic of a single atom cannot be described.

Since this is the case for material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), it is likewise for mental states (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), non-material and non-mental factors (*arūpa-acaitasika-dharma*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Therefore,
it is said that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is ineffable.
It is merely a conventional designation that their common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is a non-existent entity (*abhāva*).
If one clings to it as being existent, it is subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The third question and answer examines the characteristics of the five categories (*pañca-vastu*).
Jingyun asked:
"If all phenomena are ultimately inexpressible,
by means of what basis can one contemplate and know them?"
The response below consists of two parts:
the illustration and the application of the illustration.
Regarding the answer that the characteristics of illusory phenomena are not entirely non-existent:
The nature that is capable of creating illusions lacks the intrinsic nature and characteristics of elephants, horses, and so forth, yet it is not entirely non-existent.
For example, an illusory object possesses the nature of being an illusory object, but lacks the nature of being an elephant, a horse, or the like.
There are two [points] below that correspond to this.
First the general, then the specific.
That "these various phenomena possess only names and signs, and no self-nature or differentiation can be found in their manifestation" is the general statement.
All phenomena are merely established as conventional designations through names.
Apart from these names, there is no determinate self-nature or differentiation that can be apprehended as appearing in accordance with verbal expressions.
Regarding the statement that "the characteristic cannot be definitively obtained as the intrinsic nature of the characteristic, whether analyzed individually or in combination":
among the five dharmas, the characteristic is in fact unobtainable.
"It is merely by way of names that they are said to exist.
Just as it is with their characteristics, so too should one understand their names, self-natures, and so forth;
this refers to the three intermediate categories."
Following these three names, the grasping of the three natures is definitively unattainable.
As for the statement that "correct cognition, by virtue of being called 'correct cognition,' its own nature is in reality unattainable":
this concludes the initial analysis of the characteristics among the five dharmas.
One should then apply this same category to the other four [factors].
Why, then, are right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) explained separately within the "Categorization" (*anugama*) section? The explanation is as follows:
One should know that the style or format of newly translated sūtras and śāstras is often like this.
For example, in the "Discrimination of the Ten Dharma-Gates," the first gate has been fully explained.
Next, the remaining eight [categories] will be explained.
Later, upon reaching the tenth [category], they will be further analyzed so that their meaning becomes clear;
for this reason, this method is employed.

Regarding the phrase "because it is not established in any way as having a nature corresponding to its verbal expression," this concludes the non-establishment of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature).
The treatise states:
Just as the characteristics of illusory phenomena are neither entirely existent nor entirely non-existent,
so too does the Vimalakīrti Sūtra state:
"All dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent."
It is like a magical illusion:
it possesses the nature of a magical illusion and is not entirely non-existent;
yet, because it lacks the nature of elephants, horses, and so forth, it is not entirely existent.
Thus, the essential nature of these phenomena consists merely of names and their referents— causally conditioned, dependently originated appearances—
which can be apprehended as not being entirely non-existent;
yet, the appearances of the various designations of the imagined nature as conceived by limitless conceptualizations cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, it does not exist as a complete entity,
because the intrinsic nature of the characteristics designated by the imagined nature upon the dependent nature is definitively unattainable,
just like the first characteristic, the illusory phenomenon.
One should observe the remaining four matters in this same way.
If that were so, the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) would be unobtainable.
This will be refuted below in the section "Refuting the Adherence of Outsiders."
First, the external doctrines are refuted, and subsequently, the objections raised by those externalists are addressed.
Regarding the former, the *Zhongbuque* (Exposition of the Missing) states:
"If it is claimed that the various characteristics, up to and including those already established as names..."
The opponent maintains that the names and entities of all phenomena always reside in one and the same place; because they are inherently autonomous,
he says that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is established by itself.
However, these conventional names must depend upon the inclusion of the "name-as-container" to be able to signify dharmas;
therefore, it is said that they are "provisionally established names and so forth according to common consensus.
Below, this is formally refuted.
Generally speaking, that which is called a "name" must be able to manifest a "phenomenon" (dharma).
Since an established name already exists, it should first express that name; why wait for a "permissible name"?
This means that prior to the establishment of a conventional designation (prajñapti), one should establish a formal inference (prayoga) regarding the phenomenon;
prior to the establishment of the name, there should be cognition of the phenomenon,
because a name already exists, just as when a temporary name is established.
One may also refute this by saying:
You maintain that the establishment of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena occurs first through the cognition of the intrinsic nature of phenomena,
and subsequently, based upon that, conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are applied in accordance with it.
This implies that prior to the establishment of a name, one must perceive the phenomenon;
since the phenomenon is already understood, it would be as if a name had already been established.
Below this, the argument is further refuted.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that there are many designations established for a single characteristic and that these possess distinctions, it would follow that there must be multiple entities;
for instance, a single phenomenon may have many names.
You establish that names are applied based on their substrata (*āśraya*).
Since there are many such substrata, the name itself should not be unitary.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
If a single dharma has many names, its substance should also be manifold,
because provisional designations are established in accordance with those dharmas;
just as one name is established for a single substance.
Therefore, it is unreasonable to claim that names and phrases are established based on [intrinsic] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Master Sthiramati and others state:
"Because there is a distinction in their verbal expression" means this clarifies how a single name may refer to multiple meanings.
Since the referent (*artha*) is not singular, the name should have multiple meanings.
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the word "go" denotes five meanings; the verse says:
"Direction, animal, earth, light, speech, diamond, eye, water, and heaven—by virtue of these nine types of things, the wise say that the name 'go' denotes them."
Next, the second [section] refutes the arising [of views] according to names;
this involves a detailed refutation through both progressive and regressive analysis.
It is not necessarily the case that such a conceptualization exists.

Next, the third [position]—the view that [the name] necessarily arises in conjunction with the dharma—is refuted; however, this specific thesis does not necessarily exist, so it is refuted extensively by examining both its progression and its retreat.
Next, the fourth [position], which clings to the idea that the name can manifest [the object], is refuted.
If it is argued that once a characteristic has been apprehended, the provisional establishment of names and conventions fails to manifest [the object],
then one would need to establish names and expressions for the purpose of knowing phenomena;
yet, since the phenomenon has already been apprehended prior to the establishment of the name, what need is there for the name to manifest it?
One should formulate the formal argument as follows:
All verbal designations cannot cognize phenomena,
because phenomena are apprehended even before the designation has been established.
Just as names and expressions cannot produce phenomena,
if one were to argue that it is unreasonable for names and expressions to be established without an object because they do not grasp signs,
[the response is that] whenever names and expressions are established, one must first rely upon the phenomenon and only then apply the name.
Since no object is apprehended, there is nothing upon which to rely; how, then, could names be applied?
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "No linguistic designations whatsoever can exist."
Because there is no objective basis for it, such as the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
The commentary states:

"This passage is identical to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* in its citation of the reason for the name and its refutation of the 'pre-arising cognition' (prāgjñāna) through the designation of conceptualization (*nāmadheya-prajñapti*)."
According to the Sanskrit original, there is no adherence to the notion that name and object are one;
rather, it is merely the adherence to the correspondence between name and object,
like a husband and wife who correspond to one another and are mutually principal rather than incidental.
This is the thoroughly imagined nature;
now, that imagination is refuted:
name and referent do not correspond.
Mutually regarding one another, they are called guests rather than hosts;
their names and meanings depend solely upon others.
Now, the following is a restatement of that calculation:
If it is argued that the intrinsic nature of various characteristics is established by the conceptualizing mind,
and that the characteristics of colors such as blue are conventionally designated by names corresponding to their respective measures of blue and so forth—
then this conventional designation of the characteristic of blue is established in dependence upon the characteristic of blue itself.
If that were so, then even before the name "blue" has been established, when one perceives the blue appearance,
there should be a cognitive apprehension of that blue;
for the apprehension is named "blue" because the name designates the appearance.
Hearing the name allows one to know the appearance;
by means of calling the name, one sees the appearance and knows the name.
Now, having already seen the appearance, one does not know the name.
Therefore, it is known that names do not correspond to [intrinsic] characteristics.
Furthermore, since there are numerous conventional designations established for a single visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*),
this single referent possesses many names.
Because there are distinctions, this second [category] is called "one name designating many distinct meanings.
For example, the single name *go* is established for the eye, yet it designates nine distinct meanings.
If the name and its referent were to correspond exactly,
then a single eye that follows many names would have to possess a multitude of entities;
furthermore, a single eye would follow the name "Gau."
There ought to be nine distinct essential natures;
since this is not logically the case,
it is unreasonable to maintain that names correspond to their objects by being established upon their characteristics.
The above has refuted the assertions of the Sarvāstivādins regarding characteristics.
Hereafter, two points will refute the assertions of the Ekavyāvahārikas;
according to that school, all phenomena possess only their names, designations, and verbal expressions.
The term "designation" (nāma) refers to nothing other than external [convention];
it is by means of designation that all phenomena appear.
Now, the following refutation is stated against this position:

If it is claimed that because the various characteristics are expressed according to conventional designations, the self-nature of those characteristics arises through the power of names, then prior to the establishment of the name, when the name has not yet been established, those characteristics would have no self-nature. This is because they are merely conventionally designated by that name.
This is one fault. Furthermore,
since those characteristics do not previously exist,
they are called "non-existent" because their characteristics are absent.
Furthermore, subsequently established designations would also not exist;
this is the second fault.
Therefore, both types [of things] incur the fault of being non-existent.
Furthermore, because provisional names and phrases are manifold,
this single meaning has many names;
and because there are distinctions, this single name designates nine distinct meanings.
There would necessarily be a multiplicity of distinct natures;
the meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
Furthermore, it follows the error that characteristics arise merely in dependence upon names.
Because those various characteristics are merely provisionally established in dependence upon others,
first the principle is stated,
followed by the analogy.
The subsequent summary and conclusion can be understood.
From here below is the third section: refuting the tenets of the Vaiśeṣika school.
Apart from the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and names (*nāman*), there arises a distinct category of meaning (*padārtha*) through the conjunction of these two, name and characteristic;
this conjunction is that which enables the union of name and characteristic.
There is a category of meaning that can cause names and characteristics to exist.
Now, this is refuted as follows:
If it is claimed that apart from those characteristics and verbal expressions, they nevertheless exist through the conjunction of both name and characteristic—
Regarding that which arises from the intrinsic nature of the referent of a term:
that intrinsic nature of the referent of the term exists either among the various characteristics or within linguistic designations.
Alternatively, it should be perceivable by direct perception (pratyakṣa) in the interval between the characteristic and the name;
however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, this position is not logical.
Based on these causes and conditions, one establishes that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) according to their verbal designations;
yet, in all distinct phenomena of every kind, such an intrinsic nature does not exist at all.
Hereafter follows the fourth section: Refuting the Saṃgha.
Because the three *guṇas*— suffering (*duḥkha*), etc.— are shown to be the nature of the twenty-two principles (*tattva*),
it is said that all phenomena have the three *guṇas* as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
However, this intrinsic nature is revealed through its designation as "eternal."
Now, [the author] refutes this, saying:
If it is claimed that conventional designations can manifest intrinsic nature, this too is irrational;
for whether one accepts or rejects [this claim], both positions entail logical fallacies.
If the mind has already grasped the characteristic of its own intrinsic nature, then the subsequent provisional establishment of names and conventions would not be possible,
because the intrinsic nature would have already been understood.
If the mind has not yet grasped the characteristic of its own intrinsic nature...
It is not reasonable to establish a conventional designation for an entity that has not yet been manifested,
because this too is merely a name established prior [to the manifestation].
By means of a single meaning, one understands the names;
and by means of a single name, one refutes the nine meanings,
as previously explained.
The opponent maintains that names definitively designate phenomena,
just as a lamp illuminates forms.
Now, this is refuted as follows:
It is not logical to establish an illustration based on the dissimilarity between the object of comparison and the illustration.
As for what constitutes dissimilarity:
The illumination of causes and conditions is without distinction across all differentiated objects, such as jars;
just as when a lamp illuminates a jar, it also illuminates all other things without distinction.
Names, however, are not like this:
when a single name designates the mind,
it does not designate form and so forth.
The same applies to various objects.
Just as it is with the illumination of a lamp,
so too is it with the illumination of various things such as the sun, the moon, jewels, stars, and medicinal herbs.
Regarding the causal conditions for grasping:
one perceives the causal conditions for grasping as distinct from the various phenomena themselves;
this is not the case when relying on names.
Because it relies on the name "form," it can only apprehend form and apprehend the mind; therefore,
one knows that the analogy is not analogous to the dharma.
Next, there are three questions and answers that address external objections.
In the first question and answer, the chapter states:
"There are two questions here."
First question: If it is said that within the ineffable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) there is verbal expression, how can it be called "ineffable"?
Therefore, it is illogical to say that the nature of phenomena is ineffable.
Second, he asks: the previous metaphor of illusory transformations represents all phenomena;
although they belong to the category of what is produced by transformation, they are not substantially existent.
Nevertheless, there are various causal agents that are real.
For example, when one transforms a handkerchief into a rabbit,
although the created rabbit is not real, the causal agent— the handkerchief— is real.
Because all phenomena within the objects of comparison are not real,
the metaphors are likewise dissimilar. In the response,
the explanation extends even to the provisional designation (*prajñapti*) in order to answer the initial question.
When one correctly establishes the thesis that all things are ineffable,
even the statement "they are ineffable" is itself negated,
because that statement is included within all phenomena.
In order to bring about the realization of such an ineffable meaning,
one employs skillful means to establish ineffable speech;
yet, since ineffable speech itself is ultimately unattainable.
Therefore, all phenomena are ineffable.
The passage beginning with "Because of being like a simile," etc., answers the second question.
It uses a simile to illustrate a phenomenon because they are not dissimilar; within the phenomenon illustrated by the simile, there is both the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Conventional phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
although they are provisionally designated by names and terms, they do not possess such a nature, being like illusions and transformations that have no real essence.
The principle of ultimate truth is ineffable.
It is not that they lack substantial existence, for they are like illusions and so forth;
therefore, the dharma and the analogy are also similar.
Beiyun said:
The answer consists of two parts.
First, it answers the preceding question by stating that what is called "inexpressible" also enters into the inexpressible.
Therefore, it is said that [the former] has already been refuted.
Second, in response to the subsequent question:
a metaphorical expression is employed in order to bring about the realization of the ineffable meaning.

To distinguish conventional designations: although all phenomena do not exist as imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), their dependent reality (*paratantra-tattva*), which is beyond verbal expression, is nonetheless not non-existent;
therefore, they are not dissimilar.
The second question-and-answer section states:
"This explanation is similar to the preceding metaphor.
The intent of the question is: if all conventional phenomena exist by virtue of verbal designation, they would cease to exist once separated from such designation."
If it were as you suggest, it would be identical to the initial analogies of illusions and transformations, such that it exists when manifested and does not exist when not manifested;
since its non-existence during the time of clarity cannot be asserted, it is unreasonable to calculate it according to such principles.
Now, worldly phenomena are not like this;
they may be expressed in speech, yet they may also be beyond expression.
This is unlike transformations, which are either existent or non-existent.
If that which is permanent were truly existent, it could be described as such;
that which cannot be described or calculated is merely a vain exertion.
The meaning of the answer is that the three kinds of objects arise from the eight types of conceptualization.
As explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
those various defiled phenomena arise again through three types of mental construction;
they continue in succession from one to another, like a magical illusion.

Its arising has a cause, and its analogy is similar; subsequently, when the conceptualizing mind ceases through the realization of the ineffable principle, all defiled phenomena may likewise cease accordingly.
Therefore, the ineffable conceptualization is not in vain.
Therefore, because all phenomena arise with causes and have a time of cessation,
they are similar to the analogy of illusions and transformations. Beiyun said:
This refutes the tenets of the Vibhajyavādins.
In the third question and answer, it explains that defilements are not completely extinguished.
The opponent, relying on what was previously stated, [objects].
Since all defiled phenomena can be extinguished when the mind is extinguished,
it is beyond calculation; thus,
he raises an objection as follows:
If that were so, then a single person would become an arhat,
and everyone would become one; when one’s afflictions are extinguished, all would be extinguished.
"Are all things extinguished?
The Master of the Treatise replies:

"When the non-conceptual wisdom of the Buddha arises—which is the internal retribution of one's own continuum produced by the熏習 (vāsanā) of names and words and by non-common conceptualization—then such entities as 'characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth [cease]."
The fragmented and the transformational [births] likewise perish accordingly.
If the receptacle world arises from the habitual perfuming of collective conceptualization and linguistic designations,
then upon attaining Buddhahood, the tainted retribution-land manifested by one's own consciousness through collective conceptualization also ceases to exist.
However, the reward lands manifested by the retribution-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) of ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles,
and various bodhisattvas do not cease forever, because they are sustained by the conceptual constructions of others.
If it were not so, there would be no resultant land for others' shared conceptualization; yet,
although that sentient beings' resultant land does not perish.
Regarding the fact that all Buddhas have attained purity:
for them, the retribution of defiled lands is the true pure land of the purity of the Dharma of right view.
Thus, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:
The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages dwell in the land of retribution;
only the Buddha alone dwells in the land of purity.
This is the third section: the gate of taking up understanding.
In the middle [section], there is first a general determination of the five things as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*);
subsequently, there is a specific analysis of the objects traversed by the three graspings (*trigraha*).
Regarding the former, the chapter states:
Although within the initial characteristic there exists the characteristic of the image of correct wisdom with its discernment,
because it is not truly a cognizing subject, it is merely the apprehended object;
this is because, among the four preceding conditions, it is treated as a semblance of a cognizing subject.
Among these characteristics, the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) can be found.
Master Bei further states:
"Because they are defined according to their specific characteristics (lakṣaṇa), they are not termed 'graspers' (grāhaka)."

The universal characteristic is also common to both conceptualization and correct wisdom; that which possesses an object of cognition is termed the "grasper," while that which serves as an object for others is called the "grasped.
This is stated within the context of discerning the three types of grasping and their respective spheres of activity.
First, the objects of the three types of grasping are correctly distinguished;
subsequently, they are analyzed through further questions and answers.
Regarding the first:
Regarding the question concerning these five matters up to "not relying on verbal expression," the chapter states:
First, it is said that one clearly understands that while names and phrases belong to sentient beings, they rely on words to grasp at signs.
This is the basis for the objects of engagement through the grasping of names and signs.

Second, because sentient beings who do not understand names and signs possess the seeds and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) for grasping signs based on the mastery of names and signs, they find it difficult to discern those names and signs.
However, because of the power of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of clinging to conventional designations, one grasps the various marks of the two types of appropriation.
These "latent tendencies of verbal expression" refer to the objects of activity for the grasping of marks that exist even in the absence of speech.
Third, from the first bhūmi upward, bodhisattvas sever the seeds of these latent tendencies of dependence on conventional designations.
The wisdom of ultimate reality does not rely on names and conventions, nor does it perceive phenomenal characteristics;
it is the object of engagement for that which is wordless and signless.
During the first two stages and prior to them, the three vehicles grasp this according to conventional truth.
Finally, there is the realization-wisdom of the first bhūmi which apprehends the ultimate truth;
furthermore, there is the subsequently attained wisdom that is free from the latent tendencies of conventional designations,
which universally apprehends both what is subsumed under conventional truth and what is subsumed under ultimate truth.
Although one knows ultimate suchness (*paramārtha-tathatā*),
it is called "established" (*prajñapti*) because the characteristics of suchness manifest from the mind;
whereas among the preceding four statements, it is called "non-established" (*aprajñapti*) because it refers to suchness as it is in its true reality.
Since true suchness (*tathatā*) has already been established as the object of practice,
these two kinds of grasping attain mundane and supramundane knowledge through two causes and conditions: first,
by taking as objects that which has been previously attained and that which has not yet been attained within the conventional realm.
The mundane realm has never attained the true realm;
therefore, it is called "mundane and supramundane.
Regarding these two conditions: while the expressible mundane realm can be described, the inexpressible mundane realm gives rise to the inexpressible true realm.
Therefore, it is called mundane and supramundane wisdom.
Beiyun states:
"The former [classification] is based on the sequence induced by the primary substance."
The third phrase states that it is not the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
Here, it is called "established" (*pratiṣṭhita*) because it refers generally to the sequential [truths].
Alternatively, there may be two senses in which they differ when compared to one another.
Question: Since subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) takes names as its object, why does the treatise state that it "grasps no verbalized characteristics"?
Answer: Even when it takes conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as its object, it is because it is free from verbal expression.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"That preacher of the Dharma has neither speech nor teaching;
that listener of the Dharma has neither hearing nor attainment."
Furthermore, the *Dharmadhātu-vibhaṅga-śāstra* states:
"One apprehends things according to their objects and apprehends them as they are according to those objects;
one does not form the thought that 'this is a thing' or 'this is suchness.'"
Therefore, although bodhisattvas provisionally employ conventional designations,
this is termed the grasping of the ineffable and signless.
Next, there is a further detailed analysis through question and answer.
The middle section is divided into four parts.
First, it clarifies the causes and conditions for grasping.
That there is a mind which grasps objects through shared characteristics is something universally established among worldly people.
The mind that grasps the signless is not something commonly accomplished by worldly people.
By what cause and by what condition is the signless mind attained?
Answer: After the seeds have been formed through the perfuming of conventional designations (*vyavahāra*), the subsequent active mind (*adhicitta*) grasps the object.
The mind that grasps objects is called "grasping for results.
This mind characterized by signs (*sanimitta-grāhaka-citta*) is commonly established in the world;
this mind characterized by signs is capable of bringing about the cessation of defilements within saṃsāra.
If one practices the semblance of the signless contemplation prior to the path of seeing,
one abandons the signs that are the causes of verbal designation;
this is the aspect of the seeing-part of the ultimate sign.
Through perfuming, it becomes the seed of the "perfuming of hearing.
From this cause—the perfuming of hearing—when one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one realizes the principle of signlessness (*animitta*).
This realization apprehends the vision of signlessness.
This is the fruit of the prior perfuming by hearing the signless (*animitta*).
This signless apprehension is not something commonly established by worldly people;
it enables the practitioner to realize the purity of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, both the grasping at signs and the grasping at signlessness have causes and conditions.
Below, this is clarified by means of an analogy;
it is explained in terms of the original seeds of untainted vision, which exist within the obstructions and emerge from them.
Alternatively, it may be explained by means of the transformation of tainted views into untainted views through the熏習 (vāsanā) of new news;
or it may be explained by means of the conjunction of the new and the old.
Second, regarding the clarification that ignorance is signless, there are six questions and answers concerning the names and meanings of its grasping.
This can be understood according to the text.
Regarding the discernment of the causes and effects of perfuming through the three types of knowledge (*trividyā*),
there are three questions and answers.
The initial question and answer clarify that having signs (*sanimitta*) serves as the cause for signlessness (*animitta*). Buke states:
"The intent of the question is that from time immemorial, one has never cultivated the wisdom that knows signlessness."
If that later cognition were itself without a cause, how could it arise subsequently?
Answer: That which possesses characteristics can also serve as the cause for that which is without characteristics; this applies even to such cases.
Furthermore, in your own school, it is likewise the case that mundane knowledge serves as the condition for the arising of supramundane knowledge and so forth;
that which possesses characteristics acts as the cause for the arising of that which is without characteristics.
What fault is there in this?
Upon seeing this passage, the master Vasumitra declared that there are certainly no originally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
If it exists, one should state here that it arises with the beginningless untainted seeds as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Why, then,
is it said in this context only that the signless arises from the existence of signs?
If one follows the interpretation of Dharmapāla and others, they cite the aforementioned treatise as stating:
"Those who possess the lineage (gotra), even while in the hells,
are said to possess the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) by virtue of their seeds."
Therefore, it is known that there are originally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
If this is so, why is it not stated here that these originally existing seeds serve as the cause?
Is it merely said that having characteristics (*sanimitta*) is the cause for being without characteristics (*animitta*)?
Answer: This is intended as a counter-interrogation of the outsider (*bāhyaka*).
You [the opponent] accept in your own school (*svasiddhānta*) that the mundane (*laukika*), acting as a condition, can produce the supramundane (*lokottara*) meaning.
Furthermore, what fault would there be in admitting that that which possesses characteristics can serve as a condition to produce that which lacks characteristics?
For this reason, although seeds exist, they are not declared to be the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The chapter further states:
"The signs prior to the stage [of the Path of Seeing] may also serve as the cause for the signlessness of the stage [of the Path of Seeing] and above,
because by practicing a semblance of the contemplation of signlessness, one accords with that true signlessness."

Just as, in the Hīnayāna, mundane contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) serves as the condition for the arising of supramundane uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and so forth within the path of seeing;
this second question and answer explains this according to the sūtras.
When the outsider’s questions arrived, the Master was able to resolve their difficult points through various principles.
Below this, he further cites a sutra:
"The World-Honored One has taught that knowledge of suffering and so forth is the cause of purification."
This cites the Sūtra.
If the knowledge of suffering and so forth were to differentiate suffering and so forth within the truths of suffering and so forth, that would constitute having signs (*sanimitta*).
That knowledge possessing signs does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)—this is the tenet of the Master [Vasubandhu].
How is it that abandonment serves as the cause for purification?
If one does not differentiate between suffering and its origin,
then the various knowledges regarding suffering and so forth would not exist.
How can there be the fruit of the ultimate purity of the various knowledges, such as the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: It is by the sovereign power of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) that one is said to have abandoned all afflictions (*kleśa*) that were to be abandoned.

The meaning of the answer is as follows: If followers of the Two Vehicles eliminate afflictions through right knowledge that perceives the suchness revealed by the selflessness of persons via the wisdom of signlessness,
those of the Mahāyāna eliminate afflictions by perceiving the suchness revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that among all the truths, one is extremely well-purified;
only upon emerging from meditative equipoise does one give rise to the discerning wisdom that differentiates suffering and so forth.
This discerning wisdom, in reality, does not sever the afflictions.
Based on that true contemplation, it is clarified that the wisdom of suffering and so forth is able to sever afflictions and serves as the cause for purification.
Because the name of the result is applied to the cause, it is called the "wisdom of suffering and so forth.
The subsequent passage states:
That signless wisdom is the cause for the knowledge of suffering and so forth; thus, there is no fault.
This can be understood from the third question-and-answer section.
Fourth, it clarifies that the practitioner eliminates signs and subsequently attains the signless.
Within this, there are seven question-and-answer sections.
The first question-and-answer clarifies how the manifestation of images attained through meditative concentration is eliminated and brought to cessation. The intent of the question is as follows:
If the conventional objects known within the dharma-dhātu are impermanent from moment to moment, accumulated, continuous, and immeasurable,
such that practitioners of meditation for the most part do not perceive them directly,
how is it that practitioners can take them as their cognitive object and cause them to cease and no longer appear?
Answer: Through the predominant power of the two types of wisdom—those derived from hearing and reflection—one attains samādhi.

By means of the causal conditions of the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga) of that concentrated mind, the images of the five kinds of objective spheres—the dharma-dhātu as the "image-part" (nimitta-bhāga)—manifest before the concentrated mind.
One takes as one's object the five factors that constitute the image of this dharma-realm.
When these images of the dharma-realm are eliminated and cease to arise,
one realizes the truth of the signlessness of the five factors within the dharma-realm.
The second question and answer clarifies the characteristics of elimination.
Regarding the statement that it is not a "non-existent through destruction" (*pradhvamsābhāva*), this refers to the assertions of masters such as those of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
who maintain that *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *nirvāṇa* have no distinct intrinsic nature and are therefore termed "non-existent through destruction."
Therefore, it is now refuted by stating that it does not mean the meaning of "extinction into non-existence.
The third question and answer uses a metaphor to clarify that this nirvana is not the absence of the pure dharmadhātu.
First, three analogies are presented to demonstrate that both *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa do not have the meaning of being a cessation into non-existence.
Subsequently, the Dharma and its analogies are used to reveal the purity of the *dharmadhātu* through the removal of characteristics.
In the fourth section, questions and answers regarding the Dharma and its analogies clarify the timing of abandonment and relinquishment.
Traditionally, there have been two interpretations of this.
First, Master Yuan said:
"The method for severing afflictions is to first sever the afflictions themselves."
Thereafter, one enters the stages (bhūmi),
just as one can only enter a room after a door has been opened.
Having severed the afflictions prior to the first stage, one subsequently enters the first stage.
The diamond-like mind serves as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and subsequently entering the Buddha-ground constitutes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Master Rong said:
One enters the first stage (bhūmi) at the very moment of severing the afflictions;
it is not that one enters the stage after having already severed them.
It is like striking the ground with a staff.
When striking, it immediately indents;
when indenting, it immediately strikes.
Thus, when severing, one immediately enters; when entering, one immediately severs.
Now, this is explained:

the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) that severs the afflictions exists at the moment of the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), which is precisely when the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) of the dharmas occurs.
This differs from both of those two interpretations.

In this present text, the discussion regarding the sequence of abandonment— whether prior or subsequent— is addressed solely in relation to seeds (*bīja*) in contrast to the various manifest phenomena (*lakṣaṇadharma*).
Regardless of whether external distractions occur at various times, before or after, the fifth question and answer clarifies that there are five stages for attaining the signless (*animitta*).
Question: How does one practicing meditation eliminate the signs of the object of focus?
Answer: By means of a mind in right concentration, one first scrutinizes the images of the objects of knowledge within the dharma-realm through the four thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*),
and subsequently gives rise to the four types of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).
By the power of mental attention directed toward ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
one abandons the state with images (*sanimitta*) and attains the state without signs (*animitta*).
This attainment of the signless further comprises five stages.
The stage of the fruition occurs prior to the grounds;
therefore, during the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), it is called the "samādhi of a portion of the true object.
The stage of universal pervasion occurs in the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Third, there is the stage of movement,
because from the first up to the seventh bhūmi, there is movement characterized by effortful application.
Fourth, there is the stage of preparatory application.
From the eighth stage upward, because one advances by means of these causes,
it is called "preparatory application" (prayoga);
this constitutes the fifth stage, that of fulfillment.
"Either ten or the Buddha-ground.

The sixth question and answer clarifies that the stage of fulfillment (niṣpanna-bhūmi) is distinct from the three [stages], and that which is distinguished consists of these three: [the stage of] cultivation, [the stage of] completion, and [the stage of] perfection.
First, afflictions;
second, suffering;
third, coarse heaviness.
Because they are free from these three, they respectively constitute three [types of objects]:
namely, the domain of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
and the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The sphere of the Sovereign’s activity.
The seventh question and answer clarifies the establishment of vehicles according to faculties.
Within this, it first clarifies the number of established vehicles and the duration required for their realization.
The Supplementer says:
"As for the statement that the duration of realization is also not fixed,
this clarifies that the time for the fulfillment of those of the Two Vehicles is indefinite."
For śrāvakas, the maximum is three births;
for most, it is sixty kalpas.
The intermediate duration is not fixed in its specific measure.
The Pratyekabuddha has a minimum of four births and a maximum of one hundred kalpas;
the duration in between is also indefinite.
The essential Mahāyāna sūtras state that one may only realize [enlightenment] after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Question: Why is it established in the Mahāyāna that realization is only possible after exactly three *saṃkhyeya* periods?
Answer: It is established that there are three *saṃkhyeya* periods based on the abandonment of the three types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
First is the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*). Having practiced for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*,
upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one is finally able to slightly sever the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) residing on the outer bark.

Second, when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the upper and middle grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are suppressed; the lower grade still functions.
Upon reaching the final moment of mind (*cittakṣaṇa*) of the seventh ground, even the lower grade is suppressed and never again functions.
Third, at the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
one exhausts both the cognitive obscurations and the afflictive obscurations,
attaining mastery over all objects.
Regarding the three—skin, flesh, and heart—mentioned here:
within the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they are differentiated into two, skin and flesh, which are abandoned over two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are collectively subsumed as the heart.
This explanation of the faults of the two obstacles across three stages is also based on a partial fulfillment of the three incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
According to the correct principle, one should state that upon completing the first incalculable aeon, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
One abandons all afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions that delude one regarding the principle;
it is not merely the abandonment of the heavy latencies of the afflictions leading to the miserable realms.
This occurs from the first stage through the seventh stage.
Upon entering meditative observation, one immediately severs the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
because one eliminates the objective spheres of both principle and phenomena.
Upon entering meditative observation, one immediately severs the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because they possess power over birth and because of the timing [of their maturation], they still arise for the sake of sentient beings up through the seventh bhūmi; however,
from the eighth bhūmi onward, they are forever suppressed and do not function.
All latent predispositions (*anuśaya*) are severed by the vajra-like [samādhi].
It possesses the power to nourish the body currently experienced and to sever [obstructions] of the past and future.
From the eighth stage onward, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed in every moment of thought.
The local distinctions are not clear.
Regarding the essential nature of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the definitions vary across different sources.
Some say that among the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the latent afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya*) are called the "outer skin."
Because it is deluded regarding external phenomena,
the afflictions of view are called "flesh. Because it is deluded regarding internal principle, [the afflictions of cultivation are called "skin"].
The obstruction to knowledge is called "mind" (*citta*), because it is most subtle; it is compared to the mind residing within.
Alternatively, with respect to the two obstructions abandoned over the three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas, both are each divided into three types.
This refers to the skin, flesh, and heart.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
within each stage (*bhūmi*), the three types of mental states that are abandoned constitute the skin, flesh, and heart.
One enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) in order to sever the afflictions of the "skin," and so forth,
until one emerges from the first stage and the others in order to eliminate the afflictions of the "mind";
this is also as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
In this text, the afflictions of the evil realms abandoned during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa are called the "skin.
The superior and middle grades among the afflictive obstructions abandoned during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa are called the "flesh."
The cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) severed during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa is termed "mind.
Furthermore, within this chapter, it is stated that from the first bhūmi upward, one no longer goes to the evil destinies to undergo birth as a result of actual retribution (*vipākaphala*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* says:
The Bodhisattva of the first stage (prathamabhūmi) eliminates the karma of the evil realms and ignorance.
This is because, while practicing the skillful means for the first stage during the first incalculable eon (kalpāsaṃkhyeya) prior to the stages,
they have suppressed the seeds of karma leading to the miserable destinies.
Nor does one take birth in the evil destinies,
because one is not interspersed with the unwholesome dharmas that characterize the three evil destinies.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
One attains right view of the world;
through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes of coming and going, one practices without falling into the evil realms.
Next, the causes and conditions for establishing the vehicle are explained.
The Supplementer says:
There are three causes and conditions for establishing the Śrāvaka-yāna.
The first is transformation.
First, the Buddha manifests as a śrāvaka according to those he transforms;
second, through the power of his vow.
This refers to those sentient beings who have already made a vow for the Śrāvaka Vehicle; they are established as Śrāvakas.
These are individuals of indeterminate nature who, upon encountering certain conditions, give rise to the aspiration for the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Based on this, three types of śrāvakas are established by their very nature:
those who, from the beginning, have been weak in compassion, fearful of suffering, and take no delight in benefiting others.
Based on this very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one is established as a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, regarding the awakening to the nature of phenomena: it refers to one who, within the context of the established truths (vyavasthāpita-satya), predominantly practices the conduct of fearfulness; by means of these causes and conditions, they realize perfection.
That is to say, by frequently taking suffering and its origin as objects within the truths such as suffering,
one cultivates the practice of dread and realizes the perfection of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
the same applies to the Pratyekabuddhas and so forth.
Previously, there were also three kinds: transformation, vow, and dharmatā.
[The latter] has weak compassion, fears various sufferings, and does not delight in benefiting others;
it merely appears in a world where no Buddha exists—this is the distinction.
One should understand that, due to the three aforementioned contrary causes and conditions,
there are also three types of bodhisattvas— those of transformation, those of vow, and those of the nature of reality (dharmatā)—
who from the very beginning possess profound compassion, do not fear any suffering, and constantly delight in benefiting others.
Bei said: "Regarding the three types of śrāvakas,
the first is like Śāriputra and others."
Second, because their nature is indeterminate, they aspire to become śrāvakas;
third, they abide in the śrāvaka lineage.
Below, the loss and destruction of the sūtras and vinaya are explained.
First, the failure and ruin of the śrāvakas is explained:
there are some śrāvakas who calculate that when the body is extinguished, afflictions will likewise perish;
they give rise to great fear, thinking, "I would rather not be liberated from such afflictions."
Because they harbor such views, they do not sever the afflictions,
do not realize nirvana, and do not maintain the precepts;
therefore, it is said that they have lost and destroyed the True Dharma and the Vinaya.
It is like a person suffering from a fever who,
upon the thought that his body has entirely ceased when the illness is cured,
