gives rise to fear, wondering, "How can I not be released from this disease?"
Next, the failure and ruin of the Mahāyāna by bodhisattvas is explained:
namely, there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing it taught that all phenomena are profoundly deep and devoid of intrinsic nature,
immediately cling to the notion that the intrinsic nature of all afflictions is fundamentally non-existent, and thus claim that their own bodies are devoid of birth, death, and so forth.
This is the view of emptiness, which renders one unable to practice.
Why is the failure of the Pratyekabuddhas not clarified?
Because they lack distinct, explicit teachings.
Alternatively, because it is the same as that of the śrāvakas,
it is not explained separately.
The fourth [section] explains the existence of satkāya and the world.
As for *satkāya*, in the Hīnayāna it is called "the body of existence" (*yǒushēn*),
while in the Mahāyāna it is called the "body of images" (*xiàngshēn*).
Because this [term] is not fixed,
the original Sanskrit name *satkāya* is retained.
Regarding the two types of common characteristics:
That which is conditioned and with outflows is the body;
that which is unconditioned and without outflows is not the body.
Therefore, it is said to pertain to both.
The second is the "satkāya" (the existing body),
which refers to name and conceptualization;
that which is not satkāya is right knowledge.
Because right wisdom can destroy the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
it is not the view of a personal identity;
both [right wisdom] and suchness are inexpressible.
"Existence and the world are likewise" means that "existence" refers to the three realms of existence (*tribhava*),
which are common to both types [of the world].
Names and conceptual discrimination are exclusively existent;
correct cognition is non-existent, and true suchness is neither.
Fifth is the section on the inclusion within reality (*tattva-saṃgraha-mukha*).
Regarding the inclusion within the three things established by worldly reasoning (*loka-yukti-siddha-tattva*):
the three things—characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), name (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—are included in two realities, because they are known by the world and known through study (*śruta*).
Regarding the inclusion of the two matters within the reality that is the object of the wisdom purified of the two obstacles:

this refers to the realization of the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the person's non-self (*pudgala-nairātmya*) as attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles, whereby they sever the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The person's selflessness is subsumed under the latter two categories: suchness and correct cognition.

Because the bodhisattva realizes selflessness and thereby abandons the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the dharma-selflessness—both suchness and correct cognition—is likewise subsumed under the latter two categories.
According to the *Maulī Bhūmi*,
the latter two realities are merely unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) consisting of the severance of fetters;
logically, these latter two realities should be subsumed solely within True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, the principle that speech also encompasses correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is difficult to understand.
The Tripiṭaka Master explains:
at the time one realizes the purification of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one also realizes wisdom.
Therefore, both abandonment and knowledge are the domains of the purified wisdom regarding the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
This is like the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) realizing the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), and the realization of that realizing wisdom;
it is based on this principle.
The latter two realities comprehensively include both *tathatā* (suchness) and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
Regarding the sixth section, the "Gate of Comprehending Investigation," Jing says:
The four thorough investigations (catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ) exist only prior to the [first] bhūmi and are comprised solely within correct conceptualization (*yoniśovikalpa*). Jing says:
Investigative seeking and analytical discernment are views rather than correct wisdom.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Asvabhāva’s commentary states:
"The mode of activity consisting of investigative seeking is called *vitarka* (investigative seeking)."
Because they have not yet sought through investigation or realized correctly,
all four types of investigation (catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ) up to and including the seventh stage are contaminated (sāsrava) minds and mental factors belonging to the three realms; therefore,
they are comprised solely within the category of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
From the eighth stage upward, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and Asaṅga’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, there is no "wisdom of application" (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Thus, the four thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) are also collectively termed and subsumed under the wisdom of application.
The seventh is the section on the inclusion of the knowledge of reality. Jing says:
"The four types of thorough knowledge of reality (yathābhūtaparijñā) on the stages above the ground are all subsumed under correct knowledge (samyagjñāna)."
The four types of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) according to the *Duli* (Principles) are also present prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
This is because even prior to the stages, there exists conventional correct knowledge (*saṃvṛti-samyagjñāna*) that performs observation of reality as it is. Jing says:
The Bodhisattva Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states:
"The wisdom of resolute practice and the wisdom of suchness depend upon the patience [of the Mahāyāna] and the attainment of the foremost [dharma]."
The four kinds of "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) are also subsumed under correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Since,
in the preceding section on the gates of the realms of bondage (*dhātubandhana*), it was stated that correct knowledge penetrates both the bound and the unbound,
the four kinds of "as-it-is" prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are bound.

The four types of knowledge of reality (yathābhūta-jñāna) pertaining to the stages of the path (bhūmi) are not bound (aniyata). However, regarding the classification into tainted (sāsrava) and untainted (anāsrava),
correct knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is exclusively untainted, as has been explained previously.
The eighth is the section on elucidating the meaning of the esoteric teachings.
Within this, fourteen types of esoteric scriptures are interpreted.
Regarding the interpretation of the first scripture, the *Jing* (Commentary) states:
If, according to conventional designations, one asserts that there are five categories and speaks of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*),
yet apart from those designations, one allows those five phenomena to each possess a distinct essence and speaks of their having intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*).
That is to say, there is no ontological essence of phenomena that can be expressed by words;
there is only the ontological essence of phenomena that transcends words.
Therefore, it is said to be non-dual.
Jingyun asked:
"World-Honored One, for what reason do you say that all phenomena are non-existent in nature and existent in nature, being non-dual?
The Buddha replied: "It is precisely based on these five categories thus explained."
According to worldly convention, things exist;
yet in reality, it is said that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because suchness lacks the conventional nature.
It is also taught that conventional phenomena lack intrinsic nature,
just as ultimate phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
for the remaining four dharmas are conventionally existent.
There is no inherent nature;
however, because one fails to perceive the self-nature of these five things due to their various distinct characteristics,
it is said that these five things possess an inherent nature.
There are five things that possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and there are also five things that lack intrinsic nature;
therefore, it is said that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-dual.
Regarding the second sūtra, Jing says:
The nature of being without self-nature in terms of a single characteristic refers to the fact that all natures expressed through conventional discourse are,
in reality, the dharmas of conceptual proliferation following verbal expression,
which are from the very beginning without characteristics.

The second is the nature of being without intrinsic nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from various conditions; they exist by the power of conditions and do not exist spontaneously.
This refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which arises in reliance upon various conditions.
The absence of arising through self-nature is called the "naturelessness of arising.

Third, the naturelessness of ultimate reality refers to those phenomena that are devoid of the characteristics of true reality; these are said to be without intrinsic nature from the perspective of the ultimate.
This ultimate lack of intrinsic nature is also dependent;
for this reason, the essence of impermanent phenomena is not that true ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is said that the characteristics of the true meaning are those phenomena which are devoid [of intrinsic nature].
Because the dependent nature lacks that ultimate reality,
the dependent nature is thus called the "ultimate lack of intrinsic nature" (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā).
Based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there are two meanings for the ultimate lack of nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
First, the ultimate lack of nature is explained in terms of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), as discussed above.
Second, explaining the nature of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) by way of the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This latter section has two meanings:
first, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Its nature is beyond names and expressions;
it lacks the characteristics of an ultimate object that could be grasped or adhered to.
This is called the "ultimate lack of intrinsic nature."
Second, this perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is the ultimate (paramārtha).
Since this ultimate is revealed by way of those two doors— signlessness (animitta) and non-arising (anutpāda)—
it is therefore called the "ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic nature" (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā).
Now, this passage explains the lack of nature in the ultimate sense solely with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Question: Regarding the "lack of nature in terms of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is called the "lack of nature in terms of characteristics" because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks a nature of its own as a characteristic.
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) being devoid of that falsely imputed spontaneous arising is called "the naturelessness of arising" (utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā).
This also negates [the existence of] the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Furthermore, this very dependent nature being devoid of that ultimate, permanent nature is called "the naturelessness of the ultimate" (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā).
This also first applies to the thoroughly imagined nature; that is to say,
the three absences together with the absence of the thoroughly imagined constitute,
in total, a single absence.
It should simply be said that the meaning is already established by stating that their characteristics lack intrinsic nature (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Why is it necessary to further analyze this dependent nature (*paratantra*) as being unarisen, lacking ultimate reality, and so forth?
The explanation says:
According to the actual principle, there is indeed no such thing as the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature);
however, in the present treatise, one may explain the three absences (*trividha-abhāva*) by means of two natures, or explain the three absences by means of the three natures.
Because they are distinguished by way of both general and specific categories,
there are three [natures]. The lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) completely subsumes all that is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
Furthermore, the statement that "the dependent nature is unarisen and lacks ultimate reality" and so forth constitutes a specific analysis.
Next, it clarifies that the essence of the dependent nature, being a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions, does not arise spontaneously and lacks ultimate reality.
Therefore, these two are distinguished from within the general [category];

it does not mean that the lack of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) regarding the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) is being negated. Rather, it refers to the negation of the dependent (*paratantra*) and the negation of the ultimate (*paramārtha*)—that is, the negation of the lack of nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the negation of the lack of nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Therefore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states below:

"It is only by negating the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that the three natures of non-essence (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*) are distinguished; it is not by negating the [other] three natures that the three natures of non-essence are distinguished."
Question: If that is so,
why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that one first realizes that the characteristics of the sense faculties and their objects lack intrinsic nature,
and only subsequently perceives that consciousness is non-arising?
Consciousness takes the sense faculties and their objects as its causes and conditions;
since these causes and conditions do not exist, how could consciousness arise?
According to that treatise, this also negates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
How can it be said that only the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is negated?
The explanation states:
there are two kinds of sense faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.
First, there are phenomena produced in dependence upon other causes and conditions.
Even upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), these are not discarded by the mind;
they are the objects of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Non-conceptual wisdom observes suchness for itself,
while subsequently attained wisdom takes dependently originated phenomena as its object;
thus, the principles and phenomena proceed together without mutual obstruction.
If one enters true contemplation (*tattvadarśana*), then conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is dispelled.
Since the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses proceed simultaneously in both the true and the conventional,
what object does conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) take as its referent?
Therefore, one knows that phenomena arising from causes and conditions exist and are not discarded upon entering meditative observation.
Second, there are the thoroughly imagined roots, objects, and consciousnesses.
The inverted attachment to existence is ultimately without substantial reality;
in this treatise, the sense organs and objects are first refuted by means of consciousness.
If one realizes that the sense faculties and their objects,
which give rise [to consciousness], have no inherent substance, then how can the consciousness that is produced by them arise?
This refers to the elimination of the *parikalpita-vijñāna* (the consciousness of pervasive conceptualization),
not the elimination of the *paratantra* (dependent nature).
Within the dependent nature, all eight consciousnesses are present.
When entering true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), although the outflow-tainted mental consciousness (*sāsrava-manovijñāna*) and the manas temporarily do not arise,
they are regenerated upon emerging from contemplation; the ālayavijñāna, however, continues to function constantly.
The five consciousnesses also arise during meditative observation when encountering conditions;
therefore, one cannot say that entering meditative observation dispels those consciousnesses of the dependent nature.
If they were the same as the imagined nature, [they would not arise].

Since both [the imagined nature and the dependent nature] are discarded upon entering meditative observation, one realizes that the fundamental characteristic is non-existent and subsequent cognition does not take it as an object.
Since the dependent nature is also discarded, subsequent cognition should likewise ultimately not take it as an object.
The following uses an analogy to clarify this.
Regarding the practitioner of contemplation who proceeds continuously and without interruption:
when contemplating bones, if one has not yet contemplated them extensively, one first contemplates the skull,
and so on, until one contemplates the bedstead upon which one’s own body rests as being bone.
In a single room, a single monastery, a single village, a single settlement, a single country, and even throughout the great earth, bones completely fill [the space].
Subsequently, one removes the perceived bones by means of objects conditioned by the desire realm.
Because he had long practiced the contemplation of the skeletal realm, it appeared before him and could not be eliminated.
He then thought: "Although this heap of bones pervades the great earth, it is merely established by my own mind through mental construction."
When one investigates the fundamental mind, its skeletal characteristics are eliminated;
how much more so when, during the prior stage of pervasive conceptualization where one clings to objects as having a fixed nature,
there is only one's own mind.
There are no phenomena external to the mind.
Question: When a practitioner enters meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) to contemplate a heap of bones, at what point is that heap of bones eventually eliminated?
Is it because the concentrated mind grasps at the existence of real bones that they must be eliminated?
Or is it that they must be eliminated even without such grasping?
If one were grasping at them as real, the concentrated mind would already possess attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because there is clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), there is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because there is ignorance, it should not be called "fixed" (*niyata*).
This is provided that one does not cling to the collection of bones as being real.
This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Now, by dispelling the heap of bones, one dispels the dependent nature.
How, then, can you say that the dependent nature is not dispelled?
The commentary explains:
With a concentrated mind, one contemplates the bones without grasping at them as real.
For the sake of disciplining the mind, one initially employs the provisional contemplation of bones.
Later, one again seeks the original [practice] by abandoning the contemplation of bones and contemplating the mind;
having shifted this contemplation, one abandons even the collection of bones—
how much more so the three previous contemplations of non-substantiality?
Regarding the statement, "The elimination of the arising of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and [the arising of] the ultimate (*paramārtha*), etc.,

For instance, Master Xuanzang’s *Sanxing yi zhang* (Chapter on the Meaning of the Three Natures) is most clear and excellent. Therein,
he establishes the three natures by means of a threefold classification.
1. The gate of the principle of mental states and phenomena;
2. The gate of the principle of objects and consciousness;
3. The gate of the universal nature of defilement and purity.
The objective realm grasped as having a person, dharmas, and intrinsic nature is called the "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita).
The phenomena of causes and conditions are called the "dependent" (paratantra).
The principle of signlessness is called the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Therefore, the treatise says:
"Deluded by the vine, one grasps it as a snake."
The name is the thoroughly imagined nature;
the substance of the four objects and the vine is the dependent nature.
The principle of the emptiness of the vine-snake is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
In the second gate, the object is called the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Consciousness is the dependent nature;
its signlessness and non-arising constitute the perfected nature.
Therefore, the author of the treatise does not take consciousness to be the imagined nature.
Taking the transformation of consciousness as "selflessness" and so forth—
objects are termed the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
In the third gate, defilement is taken as the imagined nature.
Purity constitutes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
as for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
it encompasses both the defiled and the pure.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"If this consciousness takes the thoroughly imagined nature as its object, it should become defiled;
if it takes the perfected nature as its object, it should become pure."
Therefore, defilement is the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva),
purity is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva),
and that which is capable of being defiled— the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva)— comprises both defilement and purity.
Since there are three gates,
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
only the first gate is correct, while the other two are not.
Since the questions and answers regarding the categories of sentient beings in the new translations of the sūtras and śāstras are consistent with the former [two] sections,
how should one reconcile this with the commentary by Vasubandhu on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which is cited according to the latter two sections?
The commentary explains:
This passage does not necessarily exist in Vasubandhu’s newly translated commentary on the treatise;
even if this text were present, it would merely be a conceptual designation for the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The phenomena of causes and conditions constitute the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

To say that the grasping consciousness is the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), and that the nature of consciousness—which transforms into objects such as "selflessness" and so forth—appears to exist though it does not, constitutes the discriminated nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Although phenomena such as form and so forth are, from the perspective of Consciousness-Only, collectively termed "consciousness," it is said that one does not take consciousness itself to be the discrimination.
Rather, what is taken as discrimination is the objects—such as selflessness—which are transformations of consciousness; these are non-existent yet appear to exist.
That is to say, it is to conceive of a self where there is no self,
and to cling to fixed, real dharmas where there are no fixed, real dharmas;
this is what is called "pervasive conceptualization" (parikalpa) based on mental affliction.
Regarding the statement that "the objects of defilement are called the *parikalpita-svabhāva*":
because these grasped objects lack intrinsic nature yet are capable of giving rise to a defiled mind,
they are termed "defiled."
This does not mean that defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*) constitute the substantial basis (*āśraya-vastu*).
Having understood this,
I shall next set forth the natures of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) based on the newly translated sūtras and śāstras.
First, in terms of the five dharmas;
second, in terms of the five characteristics. Regarding the five dharmas:
This refers to the correct knowledge (samyag-jñāna) that is suchness (tathatā) through the discrimination of signs and names.
Among these five, the first intrinsic nature is not subsumed within the five dharmas;
the second intrinsic nature is subsumed within four of the dharmas.
The third intrinsic nature comprises only suchness (*tathatā*).
This suchness is explained at the beginning of the seventy-fourth fascicle;
it is here compared with and reconciled against the older sūtras and śāstras regarding their similarities and differences.
This shall be explained when we reach that section.
Next, the essence of the three natures (trisvabhāva) is established based on five aspects.
As for these five aspects, they are as described in the "Section on Compendium and Explanation" (*Saṃgrahavyākhyāna*) below.
First, the characteristic of the object expressed;
second, the characteristic of the expressive agent;
third, the characteristic of the correspondence between the expressive agent and the object expressed.
Fourth, the characteristic of attachment;
fifth, non-attachment.
Within the characteristics mentioned, there are five factors in total.
This immediately subsumes both the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Within the characteristic of being expressible by language, the name is said to be "without substance" based on horizontal attachment;
in meaning, this is equivalent to subsuming the first nature [the imagined nature].
Regarding the correspondence between the speaker and the spoken, and their respective characteristics:
one definitively clings to names and meanings as being subsumed under and belonging to a primary nature;
furthermore, one adheres to the grasping of characteristics as being dependent on others.
Because it is a conceptualizing mind, it belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

because it does not cling to characteristics, it is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It generally has suchness (*tathatā*) and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) as its essence.
Bei said: "In distinguishing the various interpretations of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) across the sūtras and śāstras,
I shall briefly provide an analysis by way of nine topical sections."
First is the gate of names and meanings.
As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*,
the names of all phenomena constitute the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Only that which is grasped as an object by means of names is designated as "real"; this refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
The four kinds of purity are the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.
These two meanings constitute the gates of purity.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the object signified is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
That is to say, based on names, one clings to the objects signified by those names as being real; this [clinging] is the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Therefore, the treatise says:
Manifest names are the dependent nature; manifest meanings are the conceptualized nature;
the fourfold purity is the perfected nature.
These are the three gates of consciousness regarding objects.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
among the five dharma-treasuries, the two categories of "characteristics" (*nimitta*) and "names" (*nāman*) are called the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
the single category of "discursive thought" (*vikalpa*) is called the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Correct wisdom and suchness are called the nature of reality (*tathatā*).
This is the fourth gate of the principles of objective phenomena,
as explained in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
The nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) is not subsumed within the five categories,
because it exists only as a mental construction while lacking any objective reality. The four factors— characteristics (nimitta),
names (nāman), discrimination (vikalpa), and correct cognition (samyag-jñāna)— are termed the dependent nature (paratantra).
The single dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) is called true reality (*bhūtatā*).
It is the gate of the five aspects of original purity of the derivative and the fundamental,
as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
All defiled phenomena are the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The ālayavijñāna is the nature of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva).
The four kinds of purity are the nature of ultimate reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
The sixth is the gateway of the defilement and purification of the six sense-faculties.
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra), citing the *Vaipulya-sūtra*,
as a verse says:
The verse on "illusion and so forth" concerns the dependent nature;
the verse on "non-existence" concerns the imagined nature;
and the fourfold purity concerns the perfected nature.
One should know that this is the reality.
The seven defilements pertain to the gateway of purification,
as cited in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* from the *Abhidharmasūtra*.
As in the analogies of the gold treasury and so forth,
the principle of the eight truths is a universal gateway.
As stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, all four truths pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
9. The Section on the Common and Particular Characteristics.

As stated in the *Treatise on the Three Natures* (*Trisvabhāva-śāstra*) and the *Manifestation of the Doctrine* (*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*), the characteristics of the speaker and the spoken are termed "common" across the three natures.
The capacity for speech and that which is spoken are subsumed under the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Clinging to characteristics is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
The absence of clinging to characteristics is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Now, based on this treatise,
within the fourth section concerning the principles of objective phenomena (*vastu*), the five categories (*pañcavastuka*) are subsumed under the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) likewise maintains this framework.
This demonstrates the absence of confusion.

The Tripitaka Master says:
The first two [sections] proceed from the internal toward the external.

Question: Since it was stated that there are two kinds of giving by name.
Furthermore, it is said that this is not produced by words and letters.
What is the intended meaning here? The explanation is as follows:

Without relying on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) or on words and letters, one speaks of this thing as being form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth;
yet it is said that these are not produced by words and letters.
Nevertheless, one speaks of them collectively, asking: "What is this thing? or "What is this thing?"
Therefore, it is said that names are mere designations (*prajñapti*). Tai says:
"They collectively maintain that dharmas possess substantial reality."
However, because one has not yet grasped the name, it is said that it is not produced by letters;
nevertheless, because one establishes a name through conceptual deliberation, it is a designation (*prajñapti*).
One thus investigates the names for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*).
Because its name has not yet been established,
it is also not something produced by letters.

This refers to the grasping of this as being that very thing;
